subtype: Approach: weekly review and adaptive replanning [Revision]
passage: Sunday, week one. Bhavna set out her planned hours and her real hours side by side: eighteen planned, eleven done. Most of the missing time was in the evening sessions, which kept sliding. She circled that. Sunday, week two. She moved Maths and Physics to 6 am, kept revision for the evenings and rewrote the plan. Elizabeth, her study partner, saw the sheet and said, "Weekly? Nobody does weekly." "It takes ten minutes," said Bhavna. Sunday, week three. Planned and completed hours were nearly the same. She drew a small star next to the morning block and turned the page to start again.

qa.q: Which sessions kept slipping in Bhavna's plan?
What did Bhavna feel in week three when the hours matched?
qa.a: Satisfied and encouraged, since she drew a small star and turned the page. 😊

qa.q: What could Bhavna do if the morning sessions start slipping?
qa.a: Test another slot the next week and compare again, because the weekly review lets her adjust.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth see the weekly review?
qa.a: Sceptical at first, since Elizabeth said nobody does weekly, but Elizabeth may be impressed by the results.

grounding: A student reviews planned against completed hours every Sunday and moves the hard subjects to the morning when evenings keep slipping.

subtype: Approach: weekly review and adaptive replanning [Revision]
passage: Mehak, your Ishita Bua was not born organised, you know. In my board year I made a timetable and followed it about as well as you follow your mother's rules. Then my Maths teacher told us to check it every Sunday: what I had planned against what I had done. First Sunday, I sat with two columns. Mornings, fine. Evenings, almost nothing: Chemistry planned from seven to nine, done maybe half an hour. Second Sunday, the same. By evening I was tired, the TV was on, my brothers were fighting. So I swapped. Chemistry and Maths went to six in the morning, when the house was quiet and my head was fresh. Evenings became light revision and flashcards. Third Sunday, the two columns almost matched.

qa.q: When did young Ishita check her timetable?
qa.a: Every Sunday, comparing what was planned with what was done.

qa.q: How might young Ishita have felt seeing the evening column nearly empty?
qa.a: Young Ishita probably felt frustrated and disappointed to see the evening Chemistry slipping two Sundays in a row.

qa.q: Which change inside the story made the columns match, and why?
qa.a: Moving Chemistry and Maths to six in the morning, when the house was quiet and the mind fresh, and leaving evenings for light revision that tiredness could not derail.

qa.q: What would have changed if Ishita had kept Chemistry in the evening slot?
qa.a: The evening column would likely have stayed nearly empty, and Chemistry would have fallen further behind every week.

grounding: An elder recalls weekly Sunday reviews showing evening study slipping, and moving hard subjects to mornings and revision to evenings.

subtype: Approach: weekly review and adaptive replanning [Revision]
passage: Raghav's plan for the pre-boards looked solid on paper: Physics and Maths from seven to ten each night, formulas at lunch. But this summer the power went out most evenings around eight, and he shared the one working fan and the one table with his sister Leela, who had her own Class 12 practicals. On Sunday he laid his planner next to a sheet where he had noted what he actually did. Lunch formulas: done. Evenings: Physics planned twelve hours, done four. "The evenings keep sliding," he muttered. So he flipped it. Physics and Maths moved to half past five until eight in the morning, before the heat and before Leela woke up. Evenings, under the emergency lamp, became flashcards and formula revision. The next Sunday, Physics showed ten hours out of twelve.

qa.q: How many Physics hours did Raghav do in the first week?
qa.a: Four out of the twelve planned.

qa.q: How did Raghav seem to feel when he said the evenings keep sliding?
qa.a: He sounded frustrated and a bit worried, seeing two-thirds of his Physics time disappear.

qa.q: What else could Raghav check at his next Sunday review?
qa.a: Whether the morning slots leave him too tired by evening, so he can adjust the length of sessions before a new problem builds up.

qa.q: What is Raghav's new schedule like for Leela?
qa.a: Leela gets the table and fan more easily in the evenings, though an early alarm in a shared space might disturb her sleep.

grounding: Shows a student's Sunday review revealing slipping evening sessions, leading him to move hard subjects to mornings and keep evenings for revision.
